lessons.fullText:
Lesson 15: Idioms from the Weather 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Jane provided a lot of comfort and support for me as I was going through 
my divorce - unfortunately, a lot of my other acquaintances turned out to be 
fair-weather friends. 
A "fair-weather friend" is someone who... 
A 
can't understand your emotions 
B 
criticizes you for bad decisions 
C 
is your friend only when things are good 
2) I'm afraid we won't be able to join you for dinner tomorrow night - we have 
to go to a meeting at our kids' school. Can we take a rain check? 
To "take a rain check" means... 
A 
bring our children to your house 
B 
delay accepting an invitation until another opportunity 
C 
meet you earlier than planned 
3) While I was running the marathon, I started to get tired about halfway 
through. It's a good thing I didn't get up, because I later got my second wind 
and was able to finish the last couple miles easily. 
If you "get your second wind," it means you get... 
A 
a shortcut to finishing faster 
B 
encouragement from other people 
C 
renewed energy or strength 
4) After listening to my son's band play their heavy metal music for the past 
three hours, the silence is a breath of fresh air. 


A "breath of fresh air" is something... 
A 
good for your health 
B 
new, different, and nice 
C 
strange, out of the ordinary 
5) I'm debating whether or not I should go in to work today. I'm feeling a little 
under the weather, but if I take a day off I'll have a ton of work to catch up 
on! 
If you're feeling "under the weather," you're feeling a little bit... 
A 
confused 
B 
sick 
C 
stressed 
6) My sister and I both got engaged to our boyfriends around the same time, 
but I waited to announce my news to the family so that I wouldn't steal her 
thunder. 
If you "steal someone's thunder," you... 
A 
compete to see who is better 
B 
do something that takes attention away from them 
C 
manipulate their emotions 
7) This young pop star's music has taken the nation by storm. Her songs 
have dominated the top ten lists of every radio station for weeks. 
To "take by storm" means... 
A 
be suddenly and extremely successful 
B 
have a positive effect on society 
C 
become rich very early in life 
8) When Sarah got wind of her teenage son's plans to hold a huge party at the 
house while she was traveling, she canceled her trip. 
If you "get wind of" something, you... 


A 
are surprised by it 
B 
get very angry 
C 
learn it indirectly 
9) The hard part about being a freelance writer is that it's hard to maintain a 
stable income. It's a good thing I have some savings in the bank, because right 
now I'm going through a dry spell. 
A "dry spell" is... 
A 
a major project that takes up all your time 
B 
a period of time with little or no success 
C 
a situation where your work is being evaluated 
10) Sorry to rain on your parade – it looks like this is a great party, but 
you're not allowed to play loud music in the apartment building after 10 PM. 
Could you please turn it down? 
If you "rain on someone's parade," it means you... 
A 
enter their home without asking 
B 
interrupt them 
C 
ruin their fun 
 
Explanation 
#1 - a fair-weather friend = (C) – someone who is your friend 
only when things are good 
 
"Fair" weather means nice weather - when it's sunny and pleasant. A fair-
weather friend spends time with you and helps you when everything in your 
life is going well - but when the situation is bad, this "friend" often disappears. 


#2 - take a rain check = (B) – delay accepting an invitation until 
another opportunity 
 
In the 1880s, if a baseball game was canceled because of rain, the people who 
had tickets for that game received a "check" that they could use to attend 
another game in the future. 
This idiom is now used in social situations when you can't attend an event or 
accept an invitation, but you would like to delay it to another time in the 
future. 
#3 - get your second wind = (C) – get renewed energy or 
strength 
 
In this case, the word "wind" is not referring to weather, but to your 
breathing. Sometimes when you're doing exercise, you get tired and find it 
hard to breathe - but then after some time, your energy comes back and it's 
easy to breathe. This burst of restored energy is called your "second wind." 
 


The idiom "second wind" can be applied to other things, not just physical 
activity - for example, if you are working on a project for many hours and 
you're starting to lose your enthusiasm, but then you get your second wind 
(new energy) to continue working.  
#4 - a breath of fresh air = (B) – something new, different, and 
nice 
 
If you're in an area with a lot of air pollution, then it feels good to get a breath 
of fresh air - air that is new and clean. The idiom "a breath of fresh air" is used 
for anything that is a welcome change from your current situation. 
#5 - under the weather = (B) – sick 
 
This is a nautical idiom. When a sailor was sick, he went to a room under the 
deck (and away from exposure to the weather) to rest and recover. Today, the 
expression "under the weather" is used when you're feeling a little bit sick - 
like a mild headache or a light cold. It is not used for serious illness. 
 
#6 - steal someone's thunder = (B) – do something that takes 
attention away from that person 
 


This idiom has an interesting story behind it.  
Thunder is the loud crashing or rumbling sound you hear during a storm. In 
the world of theater in the 16th century, people were trying to invent a 
machine that could imitate the sound of thunder during performances.  
One man, John Dennis, invented a new method of producing the sound of 
thunder - however, other people later stole his idea and used his method, so 
he never got much recognition for it. This is why the idiom "steal someone's 
thunder" means to do something that robs attention from someone else. 
#7 - take by storm = (A) – be suddenly and extremely successful 
 
When a storm comes, it usually dominates the entire region. If a person or a 
trend "takes the world by storm," he or she has sudden success with great 
popularity, thus "dominating" the area. 
 
#8 - get wind of something = (C) – learn information indirectly 
 
The wind can bring you smells - like the smell of the ocean, for example, from 
some distance away. So if you "get wind of" a piece of information, it means 
that you learn about it in an indirect way, such as through other people, and 
not directly from the source. 


#9 - dry spell = (B) – a period of time with little or no success 
 
"Spell" is a word for a period of time - and a literal dry spell is a period with no 
rain. The idiom "dry spell" is also used for a time with no success in your life - 
for example, if you are single and it has been a long time since you went on a 
date, then you are in a dry spell. 
 
#10 - rain on someone's parade = (C) – ruin their fun 
 
A parade is a procession. Parades are a lot of fun, but if it starts to rain, then 
the parade will be canceled. The idiom "rain on someone's parade" means to 
do something that ruins their fun. 
 
Now take the quiz and try the short-answer exercises! 
 


Practice Quiz 
1) I wanted to throw a surprise birthday party for my brother, but he 
_____________ it several days before so it wasn't a surprise. He still enjoyed the 
party, though! 
A 
took a rain check for 
B 
got wind of 
C 
rained on the parade 
2) I had a lot of boring professors in college, but Mrs. Smith was ______________ - 
her classes were always creative and engaging. 
A 
a breath of fresh air 
B 
a fair-weather friend 
C 
a dry spell 
3) Let's bring some chicken soup over to Paula, I hear she's a little 
________________. 
A 
second wind 
B 
taken by storm 
C 
under the weather 
4) I'm going to have to _______________ on the trip to the mountains this 
weekend - I was called in to work on Saturday. 
A 
be under the weather 
B 
steal your thunder 
C 
take a rain check 
5) Everyone was enjoying the barbecue until Henry started going on and on 
about how eating red meat causes heart disease and cancer. I wish he had 
kept his opinions to himself instead of __________________. 
A 
taking us by storm 
B 
raining on our parade 
C 
stealing our thunder 


6) I never knew how many _______________ I had until I started going through 
chemotherapy and only two people visited me at the hospital. 
A 
fair-weather friends 
B 
breaths of fresh air 
C 
dry spells 
7) I stayed up until 3 AM writing this article because I had _______________ and 
didn't want the inspiration to go to waste! 
A 
gotten wind of it 
B 
gotten my second wind 
C 
taken a rain check 
8) The New York Yankees finally won a game against the Boston Red Sox, 
finally putting an end to a two-week long ____________. 
A 
dry spell 
B 
breath of fresh air 
C 
stolen thunder 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Short-Answer Exercises 
1) Do you have any fair-weather friends? 
2) When was the last time you had to take a rain check for an event or an 
invitation? 
3) Describe a recent trend that has taken your country by storm. 
4) Have you ever gone through a “dry spell” in some area of your life? 
5) When was the last time you felt like something was “a breath of fresh 
air”? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net  
 
Practice Quiz Answers 
1) B 
2) A 
3) C 
4) C 
5) B 
6) A 
7) B 
8) A

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 16: Idioms from Music 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) The businessman was against the proposal at first, but he changed his 
tune when he saw that it would make him a lot of money. 
"Change your tune" means... 
A 
change your future plans 
B 
change the people you are working with 
C 
change your opinion completely 
2) After John crashed his parents' car while driving around with his friends, he 
had to go home and face the music. 
If you "face the music," it means you... 
A 
provide compensation for something that you lost or damaged 
B 
deal with the unpleasant consequences of your actions 
C 
explain that an accident wasn't your fault 
3) The website for our online store is already online - now we just need to 
fine-tune a few things to optimize the checkout process for customers. 
To "fine-tune" means to... 
A 
make a process faster 
B 
make small adjustments to improve something 
C 
redesign the visual look 
4) My grandmother is 90 years old, but she's still as fit as a fiddle - she loves 
to dance and go to shows and concerts. 
If someone is "fit as a fiddle," it means they are... 


A 
in great health 
B 
interested in the arts 
C 
very intelligent 
5) We're planning a three-month family trip to Europe next summer, but I'm 
not sure how long we'll spend in each country - we'll play it by ear and see 
which places we like the best. 
If you "play it by ear," it means you... 
A 
decide how to deal with a situation as it develops 
B 
do research to help you plan 
C 
listen to advice from other people 
6) Sheila's constantly complaining about her job - she sounds like a broken 
record - yet she won't do anything to try to change the situation. 
If you "sound like a broken record," it means you... 
A 
don't have any initiative or motivation 
B 
have a negative attitude all the time 
C 
say the same thing over and over again 
7) Miriam was initially reluctant to buy a tablet computer because she didn't 
think it would be useful - but after she did, she was singing its praises within 
a month. 
"Singing its praises" means... 
A 
disappointed with its limited function 
B 
saying lots of good things about it 
C 
using it for entertainment 
8) I'm sick and tired of playing second fiddle to my mother-in-law - my 
husband always agrees with her and does whatever she wants.  
If you are "playing second fiddle" to someone, it means... 


A 
that person interferes in your life too much 
B 
you are in a less important position 
C 
you regularly have arguments 
9) My co-workers and I were all complaining about the terrible traffic coming 
into the city this morning. The boss also chimed in and said his commute took 
him twice as long as usual. 
To "chime in" means... 
A 
to add a comment to a discussion 
B 
to arrive late 
C 
to provide an extreme example of a point 
10) The author's latest novel has struck a chord with young single mothers, 
many of whom say they can identify with the main character in the book. 
If something "strikes a chord" with you, it means that it... 
A 
has a particularly strong effect on you 
B 
helps you improve your life 
C 
offends you 
11) We get Friday off from work? That's music to my ears! 
If something is "music to your ears," it makes you... 
A 
anxious 
B 
curious 
C 
happy 
12) When it came to the wedding of their only daughter, Henry and Jean 
pulled out all the stops to make it a spectacular celebration. 
If you "pull out all the stops," it means you... 
A 
commemorate a new beginning in life 
B 
make every possible effort 
C 
prevent annoying people from attending 


Explanation 
#1 - change your tune = (C) – change your opinion completely 
 
The word "tune" means the melody of the music. If you changed the tune of a 
song, then it would be a completely different song - so the idiom "change your 
tune" means to change your opinion or attitude completely - often when the 
new opinion/attitude will bring you some advantage. 
 
#2 - face the music = (B) – deal with the unpleasant 
consequences of your actions 
 
The exact origin of this idiom is unknown, but some people say it comes from 
an old military tradition of dismissing disgraced officers to the sound of 
drums.  
 


The idiom facing the music means to confront and accept the unpleasant 
consequences - such as criticism or punishment - resulting from something 
you did. 
#3 - fine-tune something = (B) – make small adjustments to 
improve it 
 
The word "tune" as a verb means adjusting musical instruments so that the 
sound is perfect. Musicians in an orchestra tune their instruments before a 
performance. This is why the word fine-tune can be used to describe making 
small adjustments to optimize something. 
 
#4 - fit as a fiddle = (A) – in great health 
 
A “fiddle” is an instrument like a violin. Musical instruments like this need to 
be kept in excellent condition in order to play well - so describing someone as 
“fit as a fiddle” means the person is in excellent health and excellent physical 
condition. 
#5 - play it by ear = (A) – decide how to deal with a situation as 
it develops 
 


Musicians who "play by ear" can play a song without looking at the written 
music - they simply hear the music and then play it. When playing by ear, they 
are also free to improvise, because they are not restricted to the written 
music.  
The idiom "play it by ear" therefore means to proceed without a fixed plan. 
Instead, you improvise your response to the situation as it develops. 
 
#6 - like a broken record = (C) – say the same thing repeatedly 
 
This idiom comes from the technology of the past! This large, black, vinyl disc 
is called a record. If there is a flaw in the record, it often plays the same small 
piece of music repeatedly. This is why a person who says the same thing 
repeatedly is compared to a broken record. 
 
#7 - singing its praises = (B) – saying lots of good things about it 
 
The word "praises" means compliments and positive statements. For example, 
in church, people sing praises to God.  


So, if you "sing someone's praises" or "sing something's praises," it means you 
say a lot of good things about that person or thing. 
 
#8 - play second fiddle = (B) – in a less important position 
 
This idiom also comes from the orchestra. In the past, the best violin or fiddle 
player was often considered the "star" of the orchestra, and the other violin 
players were secondary - that is, less important. So if you play second fiddle to 
someone, it means that you have a less important position or role than that 
person. 
#9 - chime in = (A) – add a comment to a discussion 
 
The word "chimes" refers to a type of instrument made of metal tubes. The 
chimes are usually not played alone; instead, they add a complementary 
sound to the music of the other instruments in the orchestra. This is why the 
expression "chime in" means to add your comment or contribution to a 
conversation or discussion that is already in progress. 
 


#10 - struck a chord = (A) – had a particularly strong effect  
 
A chord is a set of two or more notes that are played together. A chord needs 
to have the perfect combination of notes in order to create a pleasant sound. 
 
If something - for example, a book - "struck a chord" with you, it had the 
perfect combination of elements to result in a strong emotional effect - 
especially when it is connected to your life in some way. 
#11 - that's music to my ears = (C) – I'm very happy to hear that 
 
Listening to music usually makes people happy - so when you hear something 
that makes you happy, you can say "that's music to my ears!" 
#12 - pull out all the stops = (B) – make every possible effort 
 
This very large instrument, often found in old churches, is called a pipe organ.  
 
 


These parts of the instrument are called the "stops" - they control the flow of 
air in the pipes. If you pull out all the stops, you would completely liberate the 
flow of air so that the instrument would play at the maximum possible 
volume. 
The idiom "pull out all the stops" therefore means to make every possible 
effort, doing something with complete dedication and no hesitation, in order 
to make it a success. 
Now take the quiz and try the short-answer exercises! 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
1) My ex-boyfriend broke up with me by text message and then avoided me 
for months so that he wouldn't have to ______________. 
A 
change his tune 
B 
face the music 
C 
play it by ear 
2) We'll only have one chance to make this new product launch a success, so 
we're ______________. 
A 
chiming in 
B 
fit as a fiddle 
C 
pulling out all the stops 
3) Every time we go on a car trip, my kids ask me "How much longer until we 
get there?" _______________. 
A 
it's music to my ears 
B 
like a broken record 
C 
to strike a chord 
4) Although we technically have equal roles in the company, my business 
partner is more popular among our clients and I often feel like ____________. 
A 
I'm playing second fiddle 
B 
a broken record 
C 
singing his praises 
5) As for this weekend, let's ___________ - if the weather is nice, we'll go to the 
park or the beach; if not, we can check out one of the museums. 
A 
face the music 
B 
fine-tune it 
C 
play it by ear 
6) My daughter used to hate the fact that I packed healthy food in her school 
lunches, but she ____________ when organic food started to be considered "cool." 


A 
changed her tune 
B 
is fit as a fiddle 
C 
pulled out all the stops 
7) My husband helped make some repairs my mother's car, and she's been 
_____________ ever since. 
A 
music to my ears 
B 
singing his praises 
C 
playing second fiddle 
8) The documentary about the economic problems in Greece really ____________ 
with me because I spent a semester studying there in college. 
A 
faced the music 
B 
changed the tune 
C 
struck a chord 
9) This draft of the article is pretty good, but it still needs some ________________ 
before we publish it. 
A 
broken record 
B 
fine-tuning 
C 
second fiddle 
10) Every time we're talking about travel, my father __________ and tells the 
story of a nightmare vacation he took in 1976. 
A 
chimes in 
B 
plays it by ear 
C 
is fit as a fiddle 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
 
 


Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Describe a time when you had to face the music. 
2. Do you like to play it by ear, or do you prefer to have fixed plans? 
3. Has anyone ever "sung your praises"? 
4. What is a book or movie that has struck a chord with you - and why? 
5. When was the last time you pulled out all the stops in order to make 
something succeed? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net  
 
Practice Quiz Answers 
1) B 
2) C 
3) B 
4) A 
5) C 
6) A 
7) B 
8) C 
9) B 
10) A

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 17: Idioms from Science and 
Technology 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) After working throughout the weekend, I took Monday and Tuesday off to 
recharge my batteries. 
If you "recharge your batteries," you... 
A 
plan for your next major project 
B 
rest and relax to get your strength back 
C 
take care of things around the house 
2) Hannah and I are on the same wavelength, so collaborating with her on 
the project was easy and fun. 
If you are "on the same wavelength" as another person, it means both of you... 
A 
have similar or compatible views 
B 
live a short distance from each other 
C 
organize your time effectively 
3) Our English teacher started the semester with a lot of extra creative 
activities, but towards the end she seemed to run out of steam and just gave 
lessons straight from the book. 
To "run out of steam" is to... 
A 
change strategy and methods 
B 
have no additional resources available 
C 
lose momentum and energy 
4) Somehow we got our wires crossed, because I had the meeting scheduled 
for the 14th and she had it on the 19th in her calendar. 


If two people "get their wires crossed," it means they... 
A 
are in conflict 
B 
are not good at planning 
C 
have a miscommunication 
5) To configure your new cell phone, you just put in the chip and follow the 
instructions on the screen. It's not rocket science. 
If something is "not rocket science," it means it is... 
A 
not dangerous 
B 
something you do every day 
C 
very easy 
6) I bought my daughter an iPad for her birthday. She thinks it's the greatest 
thing since sliced bread; she spends hours playing with it. 
Describing something as "the greatest thing since sliced bread" means it is... 
A 
healthy 
B 
simple 
C 
wonderful 
7) We're really looking for a more basic computer program; this one has too 
many bells and whistles that our employees will never use. 
"Bells and whistles" are... 
A 
extra features that are not essential 
B 
possibilities for making a mistake 
C 
special visual and sound effects 
8) My brother blew a gasket when he found out that his best friend had 
cheated him out of $5000. 
If someone "blows a gasket," it means the person... 


A 
explodes in anger 
B 
fails to pay his bills 
C 
gets revenge 
9) Now that we've finished our budget projections for next year, I'd like to 
switch gears and talk about employee morale. 
If you "switch gears," it means you... 
A 
change to a different activity or topic 
B 
emphasize an important point in a discussion 
C 
surprise people with an unusual idea 
10) The number of our company's customers has more than doubled since the 
same time last year. Our sales team is definitely firing on all cylinders. 
"Firing on all cylinders" means... 
A 
increasing the number of people involved in an activity 
B 
using many different strategies to accomplish something 
C 
working as powerfully and effectively as possible 
11) Look at that guy wearing shorts and sandals in the middle of winter! 
Either he doesn't feel the cold, or else he has a screw loose. 
If someone "has a screw loose," it means they... 
A 
are crazy 
B 
are poor 
C 
enjoy pain 
12) I found the movie really confusing the first time I saw it, but when I 
watched it again I had a light bulb moment. 
A "light bulb moment" is a moment of... 
A 
curiosity about a story 
B 
laughter and happiness 
C 
sudden understanding or inspiration 


Explanation 
#1 - recharge your batteries = (B) – rest and relax to get your 
strength back 
 
Batteries are sources of power and energy. Some batteries are rechargeable - 
meaning that after the energy is gone, you can add more energy and use the 
battery again. 
 
The idiom "recharge your batteries" is used when you have very little energy, 
so you do something to increase your energy level again - usually rest and 
relaxation. 
#2 - on the same wavelength = (A) – have similar or compatible 
views 
 
In physics, the wavelength is the distance between two identical points of a 
wave, as you can see in the diagram. If two waves have the same wavelength, 
they help amplify each other.  


So if two people are “on the same wavelength,” it means that they have similar 
views, thoughts, and feelings, and they work well together. 
#3 - run out of steam = (C) – lose momentum and energy 
 
This idiom comes from steam engines, which are often used to power trains. If 
the system has no more steam it will lose momentum, slow down, and 
eventually stop - so the expression "run out of steam" can be used to describe 
any process that loses energy and slows down. 
 
#4 - get your wires crossed = (C) – have a miscommunication 
 
Wires are used to transmit energy in electrical components. If some of the 
wires are crossed (mixed up), then the component will not function correctly. 
Therefore, the idiom "get your wires crossed" is used to describe a 
miscommunication or misunderstanding between people. 


#5 - it's not rocket science = (C) – it's very easy 
 
Working with rockets is considered a very complex and very technical area. So 
if you say that something is NOT rocket science, it means it's very easy and 
very simple. Be careful - this expression is often used sarcastically, when you 
are making fun of someone for their inability to do an easy task. 
 
#6 - the greatest thing since sliced bread = (C) – wonderful 
 
The invention of sliced bread (which was already cut, for convenience) was 
advertised as a really big advance in technology. So if you want to emphasize 
and exaggerate how wonderful and amazing something is, you can say it's "the 
greatest thing since sliced bread." 


#7 - bells and whistles = (A) – extra features that are not 
essential 
 
This idiom probably comes from music – but it is usually applied to 
technology. Bells and whistles are "extra" instruments, not the main 
instruments in an orchestra.  
 
 
 
If a car, computer, camera, etc. has a lot of bells and whistles, it has extra 
features that are "cool" but not essential to the basic function.  
#8 - blow a gasket = (A) – explode in anger 
 
A gasket is a mechanical part that helps control and contain pressure. The 
word "blow" can also mean "explode" - if there is too much pressure, the 
gasket can explode. So if a person explodes in anger, he or she is said to "blow 
a gasket."  
Other idioms with the same meaning are: blow a fuse, blow your top, and blow 
your lid. 


#9 - switch gears = (A) – change to a different activity or topic 
 
The word "switch" means "change" - and gears are the different 
configurations in a car, motorcycle, or bicycle. So if you switch gears, you 
change to a different activity or topic of conversation - often one that is not 
related to the previous activity / topic. 
 
#10 - firing on all cylinders = (C) – working as powerfully and 
effectively as possible 
 
The word "cylinders" refers to parts of a car engine. If all the cylinders are 
functioning correctly, then the engine will have maximum power. So the idiom 
"firing on all cylinders" means "functioning at maximum capacity." 
#11 - has a screw loose = (A) – is crazy 
 
A screw is a small part of a machine, but if the screw is loose, then the machine 
won't function properly. If you say a person "has a screw loose," you are 
saying that their mind isn't working properly - that they are crazy. 
 


#12 - a light bulb moment = (C) – sudden understanding or 
inspiration 
 
When you suddenly understand something or when you get a great idea, it 
feels like a light bulb has turned on in your head - so these moments of 
inspiration are called "light bulb moments." 
 
Now take the quiz and try the short-answer exercises! 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
1) We spent the entire day at the park; by the late afternoon the kids had 
______________ and wanted to go home. 
A 
gotten their wires crossed 
B 
switched gears 
C 
run out of steam 
2) I had been trying to think of a solution to the problem for days - and then I 
_______________ in the shower! 
A 
had a screw loose 
B 
had a light bulb moment 
C 
had bells and whistles 
3) Wait a minute - I just sent you my revisions to the text, but now you've e-
mailed me a new and different version. I think we've _______________. 
A 
gotten our wires crossed 
B 
gotten on the same wavelength 
C 
gotten rocket science 
4) I broke up with my last boyfriend because we just weren't _______________ 
when it came to our goals and dreams in life. 
A 
firing on all cylinders 
B 
on the same wavelength 
C 
the greatest thing since sliced bread 
5) Sorry, I'm not in the mood to go to a nightclub. I'd rather stay home and 
_________________. 
A 
blow a gasket 
B 
run out of steam 
C 
recharge my batteries 


6) The soccer team played reasonably well, but their defense made a few 
major mistakes that cost them the game, so they clearly weren't 
________________. 
A 
getting their wires crossed 
B 
firing on all cylinders 
C 
switching gears 
7) If you don't get good results from studying grammar rules, you should 
___________ and try a different learning method. 
A 
have a loose screw 
B 
recharge your batteries 
C 
switch gears 
 
8) I've had back problems for years, but I recently bought a new office chair 
specially designed to correct your posture. ______________________ - I can now sit 
at the computer and work pain-free. 
A 
it's the greatest thing since sliced bread 
B 
it's not rocket science 
C 
it was a light bulb moment 
9) My husband loves to take pictures, so for his birthday I got him a new 
camera with all the _______________. 
A 
bells and whistles 
B 
same wavelength 
C 
greatest things since sliced bread 
10) I called the airline to try to change my flight, and I've been on hold for the 
past 45 minutes. If they don't answer soon, I'm going to _______________. 
A 
blow a gasket 
B 
switch gears 
C 
run out of steam 


Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. What do you like to do in order to recharge your batteries after a long 
day or week? 
2. Who is someone with whom you are on the same wavelength? What 
views or qualities do you share? 
3. Describe the last time you got your wires crossed with a friend or 
coworker. 
4. Have you ever blown a gasket? 
5. When was the last time you had a light bulb moment? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can either e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net  
 
Practice Quiz Answers 
1) C 
2) B 
3) A 
4) B 
5) C 
6) B 
7) C 
8) A 
9) A 
10) 
A

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 18: Idioms from Violence and 
Death 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) I hate going to the dentist, but I have a really bad toothache - so I'm going to 
have to bite the bullet and make an appointment. 
If you "bite the bullet," it means you... 
A 
need to have a minor medical or dental procedure 
B 
have to do something quickly 
C 
make yourself do something difficult or unpleasant 
2) My family was against homeschooling my daughter, but I stuck to my guns 
because I thought it would give her the best educational experience. 
If you "stick to your guns," it means you... 
A 
make a permanent decision 
B 
remain firm in your convictions 
C 
verbally attack other people 
3) I really can't talk on the phone right now. It's 4 PM and I'm under the gun 
to finish writing a report before I leave for the day. 
If you are "under the gun," it means you are... 
A 
anti-social 
B 
not feeling well 
C 
under pressure 
4) Can we put an end to poverty in the world within the next twenty years? 
It's certainly possible, but I think it's a long shot. It would require a level of 
international collaboration that we just don't have. 


If something is a "long shot," it means that it... 
A 
has a very low probability of success 
B 
requires a large number of people to make changes 
C 
will take a long time 
5) Fifteen dollars for a sandwich in an airport is highway robbery, but I 
bought it anyway because I was really hungry. 
"Highway robbery" is... 
A 
a task you hate doing 
B 
a ridiculously high price 
C 
something illegal 
6) Helping victims of abuse recover is often an uphill battle, but it's also 
some of the most rewarding work I do as a psychologist. 
An "uphill battle" is something... 
A 
difficult and filled with obstacles 
B 
impossible to do without professional training 
C 
positive for society 
7) Having internet on my cell phone is a double-edged sword - it's really 
convenient and yet it also makes it hard to completely disconnect from my 
work on evenings and weekends. 
If something is a "double-edged sword," it... 
A 
has a good side and a bad side 
B 
is necessary for everyday life 
C 
often makes you annoyed 
8) My sister invited me out for a chat over coffee and then dropped a 
bombshell: she's leaving her husband and moving to another country with 
her kids. 
To "drop a bombshell" means... 


A 
do something that could be dangerous 
B 
tell a shocking or upsetting piece of news 
C 
try to escape a bad situation in life 
9) Every time I give Barbara a suggestion for resolving the problem, she just 
shoots it down. I don't think she really wants a solution; it seems like she just 
wants to complain about it.  
If you "shoot down" an idea, you... 
A 
criticize or reject it 
B 
implement it immediately 
C 
write it on paper 
10) My girlfriend is a fashion designer who is always following the newest 
trends. She wouldn't be caught dead wearing last year's styles. 
If someone "wouldn't be caught dead" doing something, it means the person... 
A 
could lose their job because of it 
B 
is desperate to try it 
C 
would never do it 
11) The last movie in the trilogy comes out tomorrow. I'm dying to see it - the 
first two movies were incredible! 
If you are "dying to" do something, it means you... 
A 
are afraid of doing it 
B 
aren't permitted to do it 
C 
really want to do it 
12) Have you seen the new English teacher? He's a dead ringer for Brad Pitt! 
All the women are hoping to be in his class next semester. 
A "dead ringer" is... 
A 
a big fan 
B 
a sexy person 
C 
an exact duplicate 


Explanation 
#1 - bite the bullet = (C) – make yourself do something difficult 
or unpleasant 
 
A bullet is a piece of ammunition used in a gun.  
 
It is believed that in the past, when soldiers on the battlefield had to have 
surgery without anesthesia, they bit a bullet to help them endure the pain - so 
today the idiom "bite the bullet" means to force yourself to do something you 
don't want to do - or something you have been delaying for a long time. 
#2 - stick to your guns = (B) – remain firm in your convictions 
 
If a soldier is being attacked by enemies, but he "sticks to" (stays with) his gun 
instead of running away, he is being firm and courageous. The expression 
"stick to your guns" therefore means to remain firm in your beliefs or 
opinions, even when other people are attacking you and pressuring you to 
change. 
#3 - under the gun = (C) – under pressure 
 
If someone was pointing a gun at you and telling you to do something, then 
you would definitely be under a lot of pressure to get the task done! This is 
why "under the gun" means "under pressure" - often under the pressure of a 
time limit. 


#4 - a long shot = (A) – has a very low probability of success 
 
It's very difficult to shoot a target that is a long distance away - so anything 
with a low probability of success is called a "long shot." 
#5 - highway robbery = (B) – a ridiculously high price 
 
In the Middle Ages, thieves and bandits often robbed caravans on the road or 
highway. These robberies were often very lucrative for the thieves. Today, the 
expression "highway robbery" is used to describe when an extremely high 
price is charged for something that is not worth so much money. Another 
phrase for this situation is "it's a rip-off." 
#6 - an uphill battle = (A) – difficult and filled with obstacles 
 
If there are two armies fighting a battle, but one side is trying to advance 
uphill, it will be more difficult for them to succeed. This is why the idiom 
"uphill battle" is used to describe any process that is difficult and has many 
obstacles or challenges that could slow or prevent success. 


#7 - it's a double-edged sword = (A) – it has a good side and a 
bad side 
 
Each "side" of a sword is called an edge. The sword has two edges, so you need 
to be careful - one side could cut your enemy, but the other side could cut you. 
The expression "double-edged sword" therefore means something with both 
an advantage and a disadvantage. 
 
#8 - drop a bombshell = (B) – tell shocking or upsetting news 
 
Bombshell is another word for bomb. When a bomb explodes, it causes a lot of 
damage. So if you drop a bombshell in conversation, it means you say 
something that could shock or upset people, or something that could have 
widespread negative consequences. 


#9 - shoot down = (A) – criticize or reject 
 
This idiom comes from trying to shoot down enemy planes. If you shoot down 
someone's ideas or suggestions, it means you criticize their ideas or reject 
them immediately. 
 
#10 - wouldn't be caught dead = (C) – would never do it 
 
This idiom is simply a way to exaggerate the fact that you would NEVER do 
something - usually something that would embarrass you. For example, if 
there is a boy who is very masculine and doesn't like anything pink or "girly," 
you could say "he wouldn't be caught dead playing with a Barbie doll." 
#11 - I'm dying to = (C) – I really want to 
 
This is a very common phrase used to emphasize how much you want to do 
something. You can use dying to + verb or dying for + noun: 
• I'm dying to see the new movie. = I really want to see the new movie. 
• I'm dying for a drink of water. = I really want a drink of water 


#12 – a dead ringer for someone = (C) – an exact duplicate 
 
This idiom has an interesting origin. The word "dead" in English is sometimes 
used to mean "exact, precise, or perfect." For example, if you say someone is 
"dead right" or "dead wrong," it means they are exactly right or exactly wrong. 
If you say you are "dead certain" about something, it means you are perfectly 
certain. 
Now what about the word "ringer"? Well, in horse racing in the 19th century, 
people sometimes substituted one horse for another identical horse - to 
deceive the people who were making bets on the result of the race. The 
substitute horse, which looked identical to the original horse, was called a 
"ringer." 
So if you say that one person is "a dead ringer for" another person, it means 
that they have a very similar or almost identical physical appearance. 
Now take the quiz and try the short-answer exercises! 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
1) I'm _____________ buy a washing machine - I'm sick and tired of washing my 
clothes by hand. 
A 
biting the bullet 
B 
dying to 
C 
shooting down 
2) There was a big uproar when the pastor's 16-year-old daughter 
_________________ that she was pregnant. 
A 
dropped the bombshell 
B 
stuck to her guns 
C 
wouldn't be caught dead 
3) My favorite baseball team doesn't have very strong players this year. Of 
course, I'm still hoping they'll win the championship, but it's ____________. 
A 
a double-edged sword 
B 
a long shot 
C 
highway robbery 
4) Working as a journalist means you're always ____________, because the next 
issue of the newspaper needs to go out tomorrow, no matter what. 
A 
a dead ringer 
B 
biting the bullet 
C 
under the gun 
5) I worked for hours on perfecting my proposal, but the manager didn't even 
consider it - he just ____________ immediately. 
A 
fought an uphill battle 
B 
shot it down 
C 
was dying to do it 
6) The politician ______________ regarding the controversial law despite 
opposition from many leaders in his own party. 


A 
dropped a bombshell 
B 
made a long shot 
C 
stuck to his guns 
7) Having a lot of friends can be ________________ - it's great to be popular, but I 
get so many invitations to parties and weddings that I can't go to all of them. 
A 
a double-edged sword 
B 
a dead ringer 
C 
under the gun 
8) Two years after the divorce, I finally got partial custody of the kids, but it 
was ______________ - my wife's lawyers fought me every step of the way.   
A 
a long shot 
B 
an uphill battle 
C 
shot down 
9) My house has needed a new coat of paint for years, but I haven't had time to 
do it myself - so last week I ____________ and just hired a painter. 
A 
bit the bullet 
B

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 19: Idioms with GET 
 
In the final section of this course, you’ll learn idioms using common English 
verbs. Our first verb is “get.” 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) I liked the movie – I especially got a kick out of the swimming pool scene. 
Get a kick out of means… 
A. enjoy or find amusing 
B. remember 
C. wanted to see 
 
2) We have a lot of work to do, so let’s get cracking! 
Get cracking means… 
A. divide up the tasks 
B. put in lots of energy 
C. start 
 
3) You don’t have to explain everything; I think I get the drift. 
Get the drift means… 
A. already know 
B. understand 
C. will check later 
 


4) After taking four weeks of daily surfing lessons, I finally felt like I was 
getting the hang of it. 
Getting the hang of something means… 
A. an expert in it 
B. becoming tired of it 
C. succeeding in learning how to do it 
 
5) My brother humiliated me in front of my friends, so I posted some 
embarrassing pictures of him online to get even. 
Get even means… 
A. get attention 
B. get revenge 
C. make someone angry 
 
6) I have three reports due at the end of January, so I’m getting a head start by 
writing them in December. 
Getting a head start means… 
A. beginning early 
B. giving tasks to co-workers 
C. getting feedback on something 
 
7) They’ve changed some of the roads in the city center, so it took me a 
moment to get my bearings. 
Get my bearings means… 
A. drive more slowly 
B. reach my destination 
C. understand my position 
 


8) The first few weeks of college can be overwhelming, but eventually you’ll 
get into the swing of things. 
Get into the swing of things means… 
A. become comfortable with a routine/activity 
B. get better at your studies 
C. learn how to make friends 
 
9) I didn’t study English last week because I was really busy, but this week I’m 
going to get back on track. 
Get back on track means… 
A. dedicate extra time 
B. get back to normal progress 
C. reduce the number of activities 
 
10) I’m glad I bought this dictionary; I’m going to get a lot of mileage out of 
it. 
Get a lot of mileage out of something means… 
A. spend a lot of money on it 
B. travel with it 
C. use it a lot 
 
Explanation 
“Get a kick out of” (A) is an informal way to say you enjoy something. It’s not 
usually used for general activities like reading or watching movies, but rather 
for a specific thing that you thought was amusing, funny, or particularly 
enjoyable.  


“Get cracking” (C) means “start” – specifically starting some work on a 
project or task. This idiom is most commonly used in the present, especially in 
the phrase “let’s get cracking!” 
“Get the drift” (B) or “get the picture” means you understand the general 
idea, even if you don’t know all the details. Instead, you have an overall 
understanding of the situation. 
 “Getting the hang of something” (C) means you’re succeeding in learning 
how to do it. This is especially used for things that are a little bit difficult to 
learn, and take a long time to master. But if you’re getting the hang of it, then 
you’re beginning to do it well after some practice or training. 
“Get even with someone” (B) or “get back at someone” means to get 
revenge – after the person does something bad to you, you do something bad 
to that person in order to hurt them, because they hurt you. 
“Get a head start” (A) means to start early so that you have some advantage. 
We usually use this expression when there is a particular timeline for the 
work to be completed, and we do the work even earlier than necessary. 
To “get your bearings” (C) means to understand your position. This can be 
used for actual physical location, as in the example about getting your 
bearings in the city center. It can also be used to understand your situation in 
life – especially after something disorienting happens: “After my wife left me, I 
moved back to my hometown to get my bearings.”  
If you “get into the swing of things,” (A) it means you become familiar with a 
routine, activity, or situation so that you can participate in or enjoy it. We use 
this when the routine or activity is already in progress, and we are joining it in 
the middle, so it may take some time for us to get accustomed – to get into the 
swing of things. 
The expression “get back on track” (B) is used when a project or process has 
gone away from the normal or best path, but then comes back to it. 
If you “get a lot of mileage out of” (C) something, it means you find it very 
useful, or you will use it for a long time. This idiom comes from the fact that if 


a car has “good mileage,” you can drive many miles for the amount of gasoline. 
But the expression applies to using other items, not just cars. 
 
Practice Quiz 
Complete each phrase with the correct idiom:  
get the hang of it 
get into the swing of things 
get back at 
get the drift 
get cracking 
get a lot of mileage out of 
get my bearings 
get back on track 
get a kick out of 
get a head start 
 
1) A lot of students have difficulty understanding spoken English, but if you 
practice a lot you'll ______________________. 
2) "Okay everyone, we have just 30 minutes to finish the decorations for this 
party. Let's ______________________!” 
3) My roommate is always eating my food, so I use her shampoo and 
conditioner to ______________________ her. 
4) I haven't read the entire book, but I skimmed it to ______________________. 
5) I always ______________________ the cute birthday card my kids make for me 
every year. 
6) There were a number of delays in the project, but fortunately we've been 
able to ______________________ it and we'll finish it by the deadline. 
7) It's a good idea to ______________________ by starting to save up for your child's 
education when he or she is still in elementary school. 


8) These hiking boots will last over ten years; you’ll certainly 
______________________ them!   
9) My high school was very small, so it was a little bit hard for me to 
______________________ at such a big university. 
10) It seems like a lot of work, but once you learn the procedures, you'll 
______________________ soon enough. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. What's something that you got a kick out of recently? 
2. Describe a time when you had to practice until getting the hang of 
something. 
3. Do you think it's right to get even with / get back at people when they 
hurt you? Why or why not? 
4. Do you usually get a head start on your work? 
5. What's one item that you've gotten a lot of mileage out of? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 20: Idioms with HAVE 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Claudia can convince anyone to change their mind. She really has a way 
with words. 
Have a way with words means… 
A. be a talented communicator 
B. have a charismatic personality 
C. have a large vocabulary 
 
2) I’m not usually a fan of pop music, but I have a soft spot for Taylor Swift 
because her show was the first one my boyfriend and I saw together. 
Have a soft spot for someone/something means… 
A. always want to see/hear them 
B. feel a special affection for them 
C. remember them very well 
 
3) We’re going to clear out the basement this weekend. It hasn’t been cleaned 
in three years, so we’ve got our work cut out for us! 
Have (got) your work cut out for you means… 
A. the work is clearly defined 
B. the work is difficult/extensive 
C. the work has not been done for a long time 
 


4) Diana has a big mouth. Don’t tell her anything about your personal life, 
unless you want everyone in the company to know. 
Have a big mouth means… 
A. has a wide smile 
B. can’t keep a secret 
C. is extroverted and talks a lot 
 
5) I have a bone to pick with you. Every time you leave the house, you forget 
to turn off the lights. 
Have a bone to pick with someone means… 
A. have a complaint to discuss 
B. notice a mistake 
C. personally dislike 
 
6) My daughter absolutely loves learning about animals and plants. I have a 
hunch she’ll be a biologist when she grows up. 
Have a hunch means… 
A. greatly hope 
B. have an intuitive feeling 
C. want to encourage 
 
7) Try not to say anything that might offend Bob. He has a short fuse. 
Have a short fuse means… 
A. get angry quickly and easily 
B. have strong and inflexible opinions 
C. not be very smart 
 
8) He has really good taste in clothes. All his outfits make him look great. 


Have good taste means… 
A. be up-to-date 
B. have good judgment/preferences 
C. spends a significant amount of money 
 
9) This laptop is very old and slow, and the screen is cracked. It has seen 
better days. 
Have seen better days means… 
A. can’t be fixed 
B. is currently in bad condition 
C. is not very useful 
 
10) I don’t have time to play around on Facebook. I have bigger fish to fry. 
Have bigger fish to fry means… 
A. have more important things to do 
B. have to prepare some food 
C. enjoy more sophisticated entertainment 
 
Explanation 
If someone “has a way with words,” (A) it means that they are a talented 
communicator – someone who speaks or writes in a unique, interesting, and 
effective way. 
When you “have a soft spot for” (B) someone or something, it means you feel 
a special affection for them. You may or may not know the specific reason why 
you have this feeling.  
If you “have (got) your work cut out for you,” (B) it means you have a 
difficult task to do in the future. This can be used for things at your job, or 


other tasks in life – as in the example of cleaning out the basement after 
several years. 
If someone “has a big mouth,” (B) it doesn’t mean their mouth is literally big 
– it means they can’t keep a secret, and like to gossip. In other words, they 
tend to share private and/or scandalous information about other people. 
If you “have a bone to pick with” (A) someone, then you have a complaint to 
discuss with that person. This is just an informal way of describing the 
situation. 
To “have a hunch” (B) means you have an intuitive feeling about something. 
Sometimes you can identify the logical reasons behind the hunch, but other 
times you can’t explain it rationally, but you feel it’s true. 
Someone who “has a short fuse,” (A) gets angry quickly 
and easily. The small string on a piece of dynamite is 
called a fuse, and if the fuse is short, it will not be long 
before it explodes. 
When you say someone “has good taste,” (B) you’re not talking about eating 
food. In this expression, the word “taste” means a person’s preferences and 
judgment about what is of good quality. It’s often used when it comes to visual 
things (clothes, decoration, etc.) and books/movies/music. 
If an object “has seen better days,” (B) it means that in the past it was in 
good condition, but now it’s in bad condition because it has been used so 
much over time. 
The expression “have bigger fish to fry” (A) means “have more important 
things to do.” This idiom is usually used in contrast with the thing you view as 
less important, as in the example of playing on Facebook vs. having more 
important ways to spend one’s time. 
 
 


Practice Quiz

1) The department manager ____________________ and she's always able to 
encourage and inspire her team. 
2) Hey, I ____________________ you - the headphones you sold me are defective. 
3) I'm positive I told Paul that information was confidential, and he's gone and 
told a bunch of people - he ____________________! 
4) You're trying to open a business in another country? Well, you certainly 
____________________ - there's a lot of bureaucracy involved. 
5) I'm rooting for Russia to win the gold medal in the Olympics - I 
____________________ the country because I studied abroad there for a semester. 
6) I'll lend you my boots - sorry about their appearance, I'm afraid they 
____________________. 
7) I'm glad you liked the book I recommended. I ____________________ that you 
would. 
8) Why are you worrying so much about your colleague's comments? You 
____________________ - like closing this contract with the client. 
9) I love my sister, but she ____________________ men - she always dates losers. 


10) If you have some criticisms on her work, make sure to give them gently 
because she ____________________. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Describe someone you know who has a way with words. 
2. Talk about a time you had your work cut out for you. 
3. Have you ever had a bone to pick with someone? 
4. What's something you've had a hunch about? Was your hunch right or 
wrong? 
5. Describe someone you know who has good taste. 
6. What's one item you own that has seen better days? 
 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 21: Idioms with MAKE 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Gary bought a house on the beach 20 years ago, and made a killing when 
he sold it last month. 
Make a killing means… 
A. do something very quickly 
B. make a lot of money 
C. take advantage of someone 
 
2) Some of the clothing that was in style when I was a teenager is now making 
a comeback. 
Make a comeback means… 
A. be available at a lower price 
B. remind you of the past 
C. return to being popular/successful 
 
3) I didn’t stop at the new restaurant, but I made a mental note of the name 
so that I could go there later. 
Make a mental note means… 
A. consider whether something is good 
B. make a special effort to remember 
C. think something is interesting 
 


4) There was one punctuation mistake in the published article, and my boss 
yelled at the editing team for an hour. He likes to make a mountain out of a 
molehill. 
Make a mountain out of a molehill means… 
A. be obsessed with perfection 
B. have an unpleasant personality 
C. treat something as worse than it really is 
 
5) The professor was fired after he made a pass at one of his attractive 
female students. 
Make a pass at someone means… 
A. flirt with 
B. give special treatment 
C. have sex with 
 
6) This cake is delicious! Did you make it from scratch? 
Make something from scratch means… 
A. make it for the first time 
B. make it yourself with original ingredients 
C. make it with professional training 
 
7) When I told my kids they couldn’t have dessert, they made a scene and we 
had to leave the restaurant. 
Make a scene means… 
A. behave overly dramatically 
B. create a mess 
C. run away 
 


8) The supermarket was out of brown sugar, so I’ll have to make do with 
regular white sugar. 
Make do means… 
A. cook a meal 
B. find something 
C. use the resources available 
 
9) After I lost my job, I took on some part-time work just to make ends meet. 
Make ends meet means… 
A. occupy time 
B. start saving money 
C. survive financially 
 
10) I can’t make up my mind on whether to buy the red shirt or the blue 
shirt. 
Make up your mind means… 
A. decide 
B. imagine 
C. have time to think about 
 
Explanation 
“Make a bundle,” “make a killing,” and “make a fortune” (B) are all 
informal ways to say, “make a LOT of money.” We can use these expressions 
for money gained from working, from selling something, or from investing. 


“Make a comeback” (C) refers to this situation: when something was popular 
or successful in the past, then the popularity or success decreased for a time, 
and now the popularity is growing again. When the thing is becoming 
successful for the second time, we say it is “making a comeback.” You can also 
use this idiom in sports: if a team is losing 2-0 in the beginning of the game, 
they can “make a comeback” and win 3-2. 
“Make a metal note” (B) means that you make a special effort to remember 
something – as if you were “writing it down” inside your head – because the 
information will be useful in the future.  
A “molehill” is a very small pile of dirt made by an animal called a mole, and a 
mountain is huge. So to “make a mountain out of a molehill” (C) means to 
treat something – usually a problem – like it was bigger and much worse than 
it really is.  
  
 
To “make a pass at” (A) someone means to flirt or to act/comment in a way 
that implies you are romantically or sexually interested in that person. 


If you “make something from scratch,” (B) then you make it yourself from 
original ingredients. This idiom is usually used with food, when you prepare 
the food yourself instead of buying a ready-made dish. 
To “make a scene” (A) means to be loud or badly behaved in public, or acting 
in an overly dramatic way that attracts the attention of other people. This is 
not considered a good thing; it is not considered acceptable to make a scene in 
public because it shows a lack of self-control or social awareness. 
The expression “make do” (C) means manage to do something with the 
resources available, when those resources aren’t ideal. If you don’t have the 
things you need, you’ll have to “make do” with what you have and find a 
creative way to accomplish your purpose anyway. 
To “make ends meet” (C) means to have enough money to pay for basic 
expenses to survive. This expression is usually used when someone is having 
financial difficulty, so they are having trouble making ends meet, or they can 
barely make ends meet. 
The expression “make up your mind” (A) simply means to decide. It’s a very 
common way of talking informally about decisions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
made a mental note

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 22: Idioms with PUT 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Everyone likes to make predictions about what’s going to happen during 
the next ten years, but I don’t put a lot of stock in them. Nobody can really 
know the future. 
Not put a lot of stock in means… 
A. not believe to be true/reliable 
B. not participate 
C. not think about 
 
2) We got sick during our vacation, which kind of put a damper on our trip. 
Put a damper on something means… 
A. have to change plans 
B. make it less fun 
C. prevent it from happening 
 
3) After I lent my friend money three times and he didn’t pay me back, I put 
my foot down and said I wouldn’t give him anything more. 
Put your foot down means… 
A. get very annoyed 
B. run out of money 
C. take a strong and firm position 
 


4) There’s something strange about that guy, but I can’t put my finger on it. I 
just have a weird feeling about him. 
Can’t put your finger on something means… 
A. can’t identify it specifically 
B. can’t tell anyone about it 
C. can’t tolerate it 
 
5) My professor put in a good word for me with the academic director, and 
helped me get the internship. 
Put in a good word for someone means… 
A. compliment the person on their accomplishments 
B. help the person learn to speak better 
C. say good things about the person to someone in authority 
 
6) When our 15-year-old cat got cancer that couldn’t be cured, we decided to 
put her to sleep. 
Put an animal to sleep means… 
A. keep it in a comfortable place 
B. kill it so that it won’t suffer 
C. take very good care of it 
 
7) I think my son might be cutting classes. I wouldn’t put it past him – he’s 
always been more interested in sports than in schoolwork. 
Wouldn’t put it past someone means… 
A. not agree with their choices 
B. not be surprised by their behavior 
C. not take them very seriously 
 


8) You should spread out your investments among different companies. Don’t 
put all your eggs in one basket. 
Put all your eggs in one basket means… 
A. have only one source of income 
B. focus on just one opinion/perspective 
C. place all your resources in a single area 
 
9) Don’t put the cart before the horse – you haven’t even been accepted to 
the university yet, so there’s no point in planning what courses you’re going to 
take there. 
Put the cart before the horse means… 
A. believe something incorrect 
B. do things in the wrong order 
C. take action immediately 
 
10) The jewelry vendor put one over on me – he sold me a gold necklace, but 
it’s actually just gold-plated. 
Put one over on someone means… 
A. be smarter than the person 
B. deceive the person 
C. do business with the person 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
If you “don’t put a lot of stock in” (A) a piece of information, it means you 
don’t believe it to be true or reliable. You are skeptical, you don’t trust that 
information. 
Inside a piano, there is a piece called a “damper” that decreases the sound or 
stops the sound from coming out. And the idiom to “put a damper on” (B) an 
activity is to make it less fun or less enjoyable.  
If you “put your foot down,” (C) you take a strong and firm position on 
something (and you probably won’t change your mind). We usually use this 
expression with a bad situation that has gone on for some time without you 
taking action, but finally you put your foot down and take a firm position. 
If you “can’t put your finger on something,” (A) it means you can’t quite 
identify it specifically. You might have a general feeling, opinion, or 
inclination, but it’s hard to understand or say the specific reasons for it. 
To “put in a good word for someone” (C) means to say good things about 
that person to someone in authority. We often use this for recommending 
someone to a supervisor in order to help that person get a job or another 
opportunity. 
To “put an animal to sleep” (B) or “put an animal down” is when an animal is 
very old or sick, so you agree for the veterinarian to give the animal an 
injection that will kill it without pain. 
If you say that you “wouldn’t put it past someone,” (B) it means you 
wouldn’t be surprised if the person did a certain action (which you usually 
mentioned in the previous sentence). Knowing the person’s behavior or 
personality, you think it’s possible that the person would do such an action. 
If you literally “put all your eggs in one basket” (C) and then you drop the 
basket, all the eggs will break and you’ll lose everything. So this expression 
more generally refers to making everything dependent on one thing, or to put 


all of your resources into one place. People usually warn others NOT to do 
this. 
 
In the past, people traveled in horse-drawn carts – the horse must be ahead of 
the cart in order to pull it. If the cart is in front of the horse, it won’t work. So 
the idiom “put the cart before the horse” (B) means to do things in the 
wrong order – to do step 2 before step 1. 
 
To “put one over on” (B) someone is to deceive, fool, or trick that person.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence:

put all our eggs in one basket put one over on 
put a damper on 
put in a good word for 
put the cart before the horse 
put a lot of stock in 
put it to sleep

wouldn't put it past 
 
1) You really need to ____________ and stop letting your kids watch so much TV, 
no matter how much they complain. 
2) After the police told us to turn the music down, it ____________ the party. 
3) The manager is looking to hire a freelance web designer, and I _____________ 
you - hope you get the job! 
4) I ______________ exactly why I love Japan so much; I suppose it's a 
combination of factors - the culture, the food, the history, etc.   
5) You shouldn't ______________ his comments; he really doesn't know what he's 
talking about. 
6) You're suggesting we spend our entire marketing budget on this television 
commercial? Seems like that will _____________________. 
7) My kids sometimes try to _______________ me and say they're too sick to go to 
school, but I always know when they're faking it. 
8) Laura has the ability to learn languages very quickly. Now she's studying 
Japanese, and I _______________ her to be fluent by the end of the year. 


9) When I was a child, I loved our family dog. I was so sad when we eventually 
had to _____________________.   
10) If I were you, I wouldn’t _____________________ by buying a "World Champion" 
T-shirt before your team has actually won anything. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson.

3. Describe a situation when you put your foot down. 
4. Do you think putting an animal to sleep is a good or bad thing to do? 
5. Talk about a time you (or someone you know) put the cart before the 
horse. 
6. Has anyone ever put one over on you?

Lesson 23: Idioms with TAKE 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) The washing machine is broken? Let me take a stab at fixing it before we 
call a repairman. 
Take a stab at something means… 
A. find out how 
B. learn to do it 
C. make an attempt 
 
2) I take issue with your assumption that women don’t work as hard as men. 
That’s a very sexist view. 
Take issue with something means… 
A. oppose or object to it 
B. think it is not important 
C. want to know more about it 
 
3) I’d always taken the ability to walk for granted – until I broke both legs 
and was in a wheelchair for months. 
Take something for granted means… 
A. fail to appreciate it 
B. enjoyed for a long time 
C. believed it was normal 
 


4) I’ve wanted to take dance classes for years, but I was nervous. Well, I finally 
took the plunge and signed up for lessons. 
Take the plunge means… 
A. begin something new and challenging 
B. find an opportunity to do something 
C. stop worrying about something 
 
5) I’m grateful to Fred for taking me under his wing during my first few 
weeks at my new job. 
Take someone under your wing means… 
A. be an inspiration to the person 
B. have high expectations for the person 
C. help and protect the person 
 
6) In the first few months after my son was born, all my hobbies took a back 
seat. 
Take a back seat means… 
A. become less of a priority 
B. become less enjoyable 
C. take up too much time 
 
7) My daughter didn’t take kindly to having to wear a school uniform – she 
said it was ugly. 
Not take kindly to something means… 
A. not react well to it 
B. not think it’s a good idea 
C. refuse to do it 
 


8) I took great pains to write nice, personalized thank-you notes to everyone 
who gave me a wedding gift. 
Take great pains to do something means… 
A. do something you don’t want to 
B. have a serious obligation 
C. make a careful, dedicated effort 
 
9) All this stress is taking its toll – I’m having a hard time sleeping at night. 
Take a toll means… 
A. be excessive 
B. cause harm 
C. cause worry 
 
10) I’ve never been to Switzerland, but I’ll take your word for it that it’s a 
beautiful country. 
Take someone’s word for it means… 
A. believe the person 
B. listen to the person 
C. promise the person 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
To “take a stab at” (C) something means to make an effort, to try to do it. We 
also have the expressions “take a crack / swing / shot at” which all mean to 
try. 
If you “take exception to” or “take issue with” (A) something, it means you 
disagree and you oppose or object to it. You can take exception to / take issue 
with a belief or an action. 
To “take something for granted” (A) means fail to appreciate its value. We 
often take things for granted when we are accustomed to having them in our 
lives, so we don’t think about them much or take the time to be grateful. But if 
that good thing is removed, then we realize how much we took it for granted 
before. 
“Take the plunge” literally refers to jumping into water. Once you jump, 
there’s no going back – you WILL enter the water. The general expression 
“take the plunge” (A) means to begin something new, especially after you 
have hesitated for some time. We often use this for things that will require 
some courage or a big commitment. 
Birds can keep their babies under their wing to protect them. So if you “take 
someone under your wing,” (C) it means you help and protect a new or 
inexperienced person. This is used when someone with more experience cares 
for and guides someone with less experience, thus helping the less 
experienced person feel more comfortable in the situation. 
 


If one thing “takes a back seat” (A) to something else, it means it is less 
important, because the other thing takes priority. Another expression for this 
is to “put something on the back burner.” 
If you “don’t take kindly to” (A) something, it simply means you don’t like or 
don’t react well to it.  
“Taking great pains” (C) to do something means trying very hard and being 
very careful to do it. It doesn’t mean the thing is painful, it just means you give 
it extra effort and importance. 
The word toll refers to when cars need to pay some money to use a certain 
road or bridge. It’s not pleasant to pay tolls, because it’s an extra cost. More 
generally, when we say something “takes a toll,” (B) it means it causes harm, 
suffering, or damage.  
 
You can use the phrase “I’ll take your word for it” (A) meaning you believe 
what the other person says, even though you don’t have direct experience of 
what they are talking about.

of class and we've been friends ever since. 
2) I don't know how to solve this math problem, but I'll ask my brother to 
________________ it. 
3) They've been engaged for over five years; it's about time they ____________ 
and got married! 
4) I divorced my husband because I felt like he _____________ - he never 
appreciated anything I did. 
5) I _____________ the idea that government programs are the solution to 
everything. History proves that this isn't the case. 
6) Eating junk food will definitely ______________ your health in the long run. 
7) We're currently focusing on expanding our company internationally, so the 
development of new products is going to _________________ for now. 
8) Armando's makes the best pizza in town. If you haven't eaten there, you'll 
have to ____________ - it's definitely worth a visit. 


9) I _____________ to ensure that none of the food at the party was made with 
peanuts, because one of my cousins has a serious allergy to them. 
10) Make sure you are on time for your job interview - most hiring managers 
_____________ a lack of punctuality. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson.

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 24: Idioms with DO / DON’T 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) I did a double-take when my husband shaved off his beard - I almost 
didn't recognize him! 
Do a double-take means... 
A. disapprove strongly 
B. look twice due to surprise 
C. make a shocked noise 
 
2) The hurricane really did a number on our property. Five of our trees fell 
over. 
Do a number on something means... 
A. cause multiple things to fail 
B. damage or harm 
C. take a long time to pass 
 
3) The boss always comes up with great ideas, but then he makes us do the 
dirty work. 
Do the dirty work means... 
A. do extra work 
B. do something illegal 
C. do the unpleasant tasks 
 


4) When the heating system was blowing out cold air, we replaced the filter 
and that did the trick. 
Do the trick means... 
A. accomplish what is needed 
B. cost some money 
C. do something surprising 
 
5) That product wasn't particularly profitable, so the company decided to do 
away with it. 
Do away with something means... 
A. change it 
B. eliminate it 
C. give it for free 
 
6) When I was a teenager, I rebelled against my parents' expectations that I 
always do their bidding. 
Do someone's bidding means... 
A. do a favor for someone 
B. do the household chores 
C. do what the person has ordered 
 
7) Six months after the breakup, Gary is still hoping his ex-girlfriend will give 
him another chance. I told him, "Don't hold your breath." 
Don't hold your breath means... 
A. don't focus too much on one thing/person 
B. something will probably never happen 
C. you can't do anything to improve the situation 
 


8) I borrowed $5 from Tim and promised to pay him back the next day, but he 
said, "Don't sweat it!" 
Don't sweat it means... 
A. don't get angry 
B. don't go too fast 
C. don't worry about it 
 
9) I was about to get a soda from the vending machine, but then my co-worker 
said, "Don't bother - it's been broken for weeks." 
Don't bother means... 
A. don't wait for something to happen 
B. it's not worth trying 
C. stop annoying me 
 
10) I hated living in Canada. Don't get me wrong - the people are great, but I 
couldn't stand the weather. 
Don't get me wrong means... 
A. don't correct me 
B. don't disagree with me 
C. don't misunderstand me 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
If you do a double-take, (B) it means you look at something two times 
because you are surprised or shocked, and you almost couldn't believe it the 
first time you saw it. So you look again to check and confirm that what you're 
seeing is really correct. 
To do a number on something (B) means to seriously damage or harm that 
thing. We can also say that problems or tragedies do a number on a person if 
they severely affect that person's emotional well-being. 
Doing the dirty work (C) refers to doing unpleasant or tedious tasks that 
most people wouldn't want to do... but someone has to do them! 
Saying that something did the trick (A) means it accomplished what you 
were trying to do. We often use this expression when something works 
successfully to solve a problem. In the example, replacing the filter did the 
trick to fix the problem in the heating system.  
To do away with something (B) means to eliminate it or discontinue it; to 
stop having it. In the example, the company did away with an unprofitable 
product - it eliminated a product that wasn't making much money. 
If you do someone's bidding, (C) it means you do what the person has 
ordered you to do. Soldiers have to do the bidding of their commanding 
officers, and employees have to do the bidding of their bosses. 
We can only hold our breath (stop our respiration) for a very short time; it's 
impossible to hold your breath for a long time. So telling someone "Don't hold 
your breath" (B) means "Don't wait, because this thing will probably never 
happen, even if you wait a long time." 
Don't sweat it (C) is an informal way to say, "Don't worry about it," don't 
spend time/energy being upset or anxious about it. 
If you tell someone "don't bother," (B) it means "don't try, because it won't 
work or it's not worth the effort." In the example, the vending machine is 


broken, so my coworker says, "don't bother" putting in money, because it will 
have no result. 
"Don't get me wrong" (C) is a way to say, "don't misunderstand me" - we can 
use this when we say something that a person might be confused or offended 
by. In this example, saying you hated living in Canada could be offensive 
because maybe you hated the people. So you can say, "Don't get me wrong" 
and then clarify that you hated the weather, not the Canadians themselves. 
 
Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
did a double-take 
did his bidding 
don't bother 
did a number on 
did the dirty work 
don't get me wrong 
did away with it 
did the trick
