lessons.fullText:
Lesson 25: Idioms with GO 
 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) That singer is really popular among teen girls. Whenever he appears on 
stage, his fans go bonkers. 
Go bonkers means... 
A. act crazily 
B. make a lot of noise 
C. take pictures 
 
2) The author's long-awaited second book went down in flames; critics hated 
it, and almost nobody bought it. 
Go down in flames means... 
A. be of bad quality 
B. damage one's reputation 
C. fail spectacularly 
 
3) If you want to start your own business, you can't do it half-heartedly; you 
need to go for broke. 
Go for broke means... 
A. borrow money 
B. have a good idea 
C. try as hard as possible 
 


4) It's the final week of the presidential campaign, and the candidates are 
going into overdrive in their efforts to gain voters' support. 
Go into overdrive means... 
A. appearing in the media 
B. traveling to many places 
C. work more actively than normal 
 
5) My son was born 6 weeks early. His condition was touch-and-go for a 
while, but now he's healthy and strong. 
Touch-and-go means... 
A. needing medical attention 
B. unknown 
C. unstable and uncertain 
 
6) My sister absolutely loves hiking. She wakes up at sunrise raring to go. 
Raring to go means... 
A. earlier than other people 
B. eager to take action 
C. in excellent physical condition 
 
7) The Australian soccer team played well from the get-go and maintained 
their lead throughout the game. 
From the get-go means... 
A. from another country 
B. from the beginning 
C. with everyone's participation 
 


8) The self-driving car will go down in history as one of the most important 
inventions for everyday people. 
Go down in history means... 
A. be very important and remembered 
B. fail in the long-term 
C. take years to finish 
 
9) My math teacher tutored me every day after school. She went above and 
beyond to help me understand the subject. 
Go above and beyond means... 
A. be very patient 
B. do much more than the minimum 
C. have good communication skills 
 
10) Disease almost always goes hand in hand with poverty. You can't deal 
with one problem without considering the other. 
Go hand in hand means... 
A. be closely connected 
B. be an immediate problem 
C. spread from person to person 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
Go bonkers (A) means to act crazily. We have a number of other expressions 
for this: go berserk, go bananas, go nuts. These can be used for when 
someone acts crazy with anger, or acts crazy in general (as in this example 
when the fans are acting crazy with joy and excitement). 
In war, when a ship or plane is hit by a missile, it starts burning and goes 
down in flames. (C) The idiom in general means when something fails in a 
spectacular way. 
To go for broke (C) means to try as hard as possible, to commit 100% of your 
effort to that goal. Don't get go for broke confused with go broke. Go broke 
means to lose all your money. 
Go into overdrive (C) means to work more actively than normal. You can 
imagine a car driving at maximum speed, much faster than it would usually go.  
 
If something is touch-and-go, (C) it means the situation is unstable and 
uncertain. We do not know what the final result would be, and circumstances 
could change at any time. 
When a person is raring to go, (B) it means they are eager and excited to take 
action. This action could be going to a place, or it could be any activity, like 
raring to go on a project or hobby. 
From the get-go (B) is a very informal way to say, "from the beginning." 
Some people pronounce this more like from the git-go. 
If something goes down in history, (A) it means it will be very important and 
remembered for a long time. It will have an impact on history, and people 
studying history in the future will probably learn about it. 


When someone goes above and beyond, (B) it means they do a lot more than 
the minimum or what is required. They make a special extra effort and 
dedicate extra time/energy beyond what would be expected. 
If two things go hand in hand, (A) it means they are closely connected; one 
thing accompanies the other. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence.

go into overdrive 
went bonkers 
go above and beyond 
raring to go 
went down in flames 
go hand-in-hand 
touch-and-go

stop _____________________. 
2. I wouldn't travel to that country right now if I were you. The political 
situation is somewhat _____________________. 
3. In the weeks leading up to Christmas, the stores _____________________ with 
holiday advertising. 
4. Maintenance and repair costs _____________________ with owning a house - 
you can't escape them! 
5. She came from a poor background, but she _____________________ as one of 
the top actresses ever to perform on stage. 
6. Erica really wanted to be selected for the elite gymnastics team, so she 
_____________________ during her tryout and performed all the most difficult 
moves. 
7. Todd's attempt to ask Janice out _____________________ - she laughed in his 
face and walked away. 
8. Two of my co-workers got promotions because they always 
_____________________. 
9. We told the kids they could each pick out one toy at the toy store, and 
now they're _____________________. 


10. 
My best friend _____________________ when he lost his favorite 
sunglasses; he started yelling at me even though it wasn’t my fault. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Describe a time when you saw someone go bonkers. 
2. What's something you did that went down in flames? 
3. Talk about a time you went into overdrive. 
4. Have you ever experienced or seen a situation that was touch-and-go? 
5. What's one thing that went down in history in your country? 
6. Describe a time when you saw someone go above and beyond.

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 26: Idioms with COME 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Victor couldn't stand the guilt anymore, and finally came clean about 
cheating on the final exam. 
Come clean means... 
A. be very sorry 
B. improve a situation 
C. tell the truth 
 
2) I have a little flashlight on my keychain; it comes in handy when I'm going 
up steps in the dark. 
Come in handy means... 
A. be useful 
B. hold something 
C. shows the right way 
 
3) Two fans of rival sports teams were swearing at each other in the bar, and 
they almost came to blows. 
Come to blows means... 
A. be expelled from a place 
B. call the police 
C. start hitting each other 
 
4) He was able to deal with most of the other problems calmly, but when his 
son was arrested for drug dealing, then he came unglued. 


Come unglued means... 
A. be extremely disappointed 
B. destroy a relationship 
C. lose emotional control 
 
5) My sister was talking about dropping out of college for a while, but I'm glad 
she finally came to her senses and decided to finish her degree. 
Come to your senses means... 
A. follow someone's advice 
B. start thinking sensibly 
C. want to improve your position in life 
 
6) Our family dog recently died, and I need to help my kids come to grips 
with the loss. 
Come to grips with means... 
A. begin to accept 
B. forget about 
C. have a strong experience 
 
7) The senator came under fire for her history of making discriminatory 
comments about other races. 
Come under fire means... 
A. be criticized intensely 
B. become very unpopular 
C. lose your job 
 
8) When you marry someone, you commit to staying with them come hell or 
high water. 


Come hell or high water means... 
A. forever 
B. regardless of any obstacle 
C. with hope for a better future 
 
9) I know you have very specific plans for your future, but remember that 
when you have kids, their needs will come into play. 
Come into play means... 
A. become a factor 
B. have a positive effect 
C. take first priority 
 
10) You shouldn't treat your employees badly; it might come back to bite 
you one day. 
Come back to bite someone means... 
A. be morally or ethically wrong 
B. cause someone to have a bad reputation in their field 
C. for a past situation to cause problems in the present/future 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
To come clean (C) means to tell or reveal the truth - often about something 
you did wrong, and/or something you wanted to hide because it's bad or 
embarrassing. 
Come in handy (A) is an informal way to talk about being useful. You can also 
use handy as an adjective - for example, "This oven has a handy self-cleaning 
feature." 
The noun "blow" can mean a hit or an impact, and if two or more people come 
to blows, (C) it means they start fighting and physically hitting each other. 
 
“Glue” is a sticky substance that holds things together and keeps them stable. 
When we say someone comes unglued, (C) it means they lose their emotional 
control and stability, and they start showing extreme emotions and/or 
behaving crazily. This expression is also occasionally used when something 
fails by falling apart into pieces. 
When someone comes to their senses, (B) they start thinking in a sensible 
and reasonable way (often after having silly ideas or plans that were not a 
good idea in the past). 
To come to grips with something (A) means to begin to accept and tolerate 
something (usually something difficult). We can also say come to terms with 
something. 
If someone comes under fire, (A) it means they are being criticized intensely. 
In a battle, if soldiers are "under fire," it means the enemy is shooting guns at 


them. More generally, coming under fire means you are experiencing a 
widespread "attack" of criticism. 
 
Come hell or high water (B) is an informal idiomatic expression that means 
"regardless of any obstacle." In other words, you are determined to do 
something even if terrible things happen in the future - you are still 
committed to doing it or reaching your goal. 
If something comes into play, (A) it means it becomes a factor; it has some 
sort of effect on the situation that must be considered. 
If you treat a puppy badly, it might come back to bite you when it is an adult 
dog. In the same way, something that comes back to bite you (C) is 
something from the past that is now causing you problems or bad 
consequences in the present/future. 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
came back to bite me 
came to my senses 
come hell or high water 
came into play 
came under fire 
come to blows 
came to grips with 
come clean 
come unglued 
come in handy 
 
1. All those years of eating fast food _____________________, because now I have 
high cholesterol. 
2. He's afraid to _____________________ about kissing another woman because 
then his girlfriend will probably break up with him. 
3. I used to dye my hair all sorts of wild colors, but eventually I 
_____________________ and stuck with blonde. 
4. I'm terrible at remembering directions, so the navigation features on my 
phone definitely _____________________! 
5. It's still too hard to talk about my mother's recent death. If I do, I'll 
_____________________. 
6. Our car broke down on the way to the concert and my friends wanted to 
give up and go home, but I said we'd get there _____________________! 
7. Some of my relatives are on opposite sides of the political spectrum, and 
I'm worried they'll _____________________ during the holidays. 
8. The new standardized exams _____________________ as many teachers said 
they failed to measure student ability accurately. 
9. It's harder to dominate the market because a few new competitors in 
our industry _____________________ last year. 


10. 
I started feeling better once I _____________________ the fact that I 
couldn't change the mistakes I made in the past. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Talk about a time you (or someone else) came clean. 
2. What's something that comes in handy in your everyday life? 
3. Describe a time when you had to come to grips with something. 
4. Have you or someone you know ever come under fire? 
5. What's something you're determined to do come hell or high water? 
6. Have you ever had something come back to bite you? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net

2. come clean 
3. came to my senses 
4. come in handy

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 27: Idioms with GIVE 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Sorry I missed the meeting - could you give me a rundown of what was 
discussed? 
Give someone a rundown means... 
A. explain a summary 
B. provide notes 
C. remind the person 
 
2) I don't like walking past that abandoned old house at night. It gives me the 
creeps. 
Give me the creeps means... 
A. cause me to get lost 
B. make me scared/uncomfortable 
C. result in anger 
 
3) After waiting for the repairman for over an hour, my mother called his 
supervisor and gave him a piece of her mind. 
Give someone a piece of your mind means... 
A. make a suggestion 
B. strongly criticize 
C. talk about an experience 
 
4) The mayor gives lip service to plans to provide affordable housing, but he 
keeps approving the construction of luxury apartments. 


Give lip service to something means... 
A. constantly delay until the future 
B. express support that is not sincere 
C. talk a lot about 
 
5) I charged my cell phone an hour ago, and the battery's already gone dead. 
What gives? 
What gives? means... 
A. can you give me something? 
B. what should I do? 
C. what's the problem? 
 
6) There's no standardized curriculum; the director gives the teachers free 
rein in the classroom. 
Give someone free rein means... 
A. allow them to have complete control 
B. gives them good advice 
C. provide them with free resources 
 
7) I just wanted to give you a heads up that the store will be closed 
tomorrow - it's a holiday. 
Give someone a heads up means... 
A. alert or warn them 
B. encourage them 
C. tell them to go away 
 
8) I stupidly lost some money gambling, and my wife has been giving me 
grief about it. 


Give someone grief means... 
A. criticize or tease 
B. feel rather sad 
C. force someone to apologize 
 
9) My girlfriend gave me a dirty look when I told our friends a story about 
her that was rather embarrassing. 
Give someone a dirty look means... 
A. look at them angrily 
B. look at them with sexual desire 
C. lose respect for the person 
 
10) I just want a job I enjoy. I don't give a fig about the salary. 
Not give a fig means... 
A. not ask 
B. not care 
C. not have experience 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Explanation 
To give someone a rundown (A) means to tell them a summary of the details 
about a situation. Sometimes this expression is used more for giving a basic 
summary, and other times it's used for explaining details. But in both cases, it 
means to tell the other person information that he/she doesn't know yet. 
If something gives you the creeps, (B) it makes you scared or uncomfortable. 
It gives you a cold feeling of horror. Another way to say this is "it gives me the 
willies." 
 
When you give someone a piece of your mind, (B) you make strong 
criticisms. You don't try to make the criticisms diplomatic or gentle, you 
express them very directly. You usually give someone a piece of your mind 
when you're annoyed or angry about something. 
To give lip service to something (B) means to express support that is not 
sincere. In other words, you talk about it like you support or agree with it, but 
you don't take any action, or your actions are different from what you said. 
The expression What gives? (C) is an informal way to ask, “What's the 
problem?” or “What went wrong?” It is often used when you are somewhat 
surprised that the problem occurred, or annoyed at a problem. 
To give somebody free rein (A) means to give them complete control, 
complete freedom to do whatever they want. Reins are the straps used to 
control a horse, so if you loosen the reins, you allow the horse to go wherever 
it wants.  


If you give somebody a heads up, (A) it means you alert them or warn them 
about something that will happen in the future. It could be something bad, or 
it could be something neutral - like giving a coworker a heads up that a 
meeting was rescheduled. 
To give someone grief (A) means to criticize or tease the person. We usually 
give people grief about bad or stupid things that person did. It can be more 
serious (criticizing angrily) or it can be more light-hearted (playfully teasing 
and reminding). 
If you give someone a dirty look, (A) it means you look at the person angrily. 
It's common to give someone a dirty look when they are doing something we 
disapprove of, but we don't want to say it directly - we want them to see our 
angry facial expression and understand that they should stop or that they've 
done something bad. 
 
When you don't give a fig about something, (B) it means you completely 
don't care about it. There are several other expressions for this. “I don't give a 
fig” is more neutral or innocent, and “I don't give a damn/crap/shit” are 
stronger and more offensive. 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
don't give a fig 
give me a dirty look 
give me free rein 
give him a piece of my mind 
give me a heads up 
give me grief 
give lip service 
give me a rundown 
give me the creeps 
what gives? 
 
1. I just had my keys in my hand, and now I can't find them - 
______________________ 
2. It's been three months and he still hasn't paid back the money I lent 
him. Next time I see him, I'm going to ______________________. 
3. My manager says he trusts my judgment, so he'll ______________________ on 
this project. 
4. Nate and Kathy are so inconsiderate. They ______________________ about 
other people's feelings. 
5. OK, I'm ready to help with the party preparation. ______________________ of 
what you have planned so far. 
6. Oops - I borrowed my sister's jacket and then spilled red wine on it. I 
know she's going to ______________________ about this. 
7. Some religious leaders ______________________ to morals and rules but don't 
follow them personally. 
8. Teachers always ______________________ when I contradict or correct them 
in front of the class. 
9. We'll meet in front of the bus station at 4. Please ______________________ if 
your plans change. 
10. 
I refuse to buy a house next to a graveyard. All those tombstones 
______________________. 


Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. What's one thing that gives you the creeps? 
2. Describe a time you've given someone a piece of your mind. 
3. When was the last time someone gave you a heads up? 
4. Talk about a situation when someone gave you grief. 
5. What's something you don't give a fig about? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net

2. give him a piece of my mind 
3. give me free rein 
4. don't give a fig 
5. give me a rundown 
6. give me grief 
7. give lip service 
8. give me a dirty look 
9. give me a heads up 
10.

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 28: Idioms with KEEP 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) Keep me posted on your travel plans so that I know what time to pick you 
up from the train station. 
Keep someone posted means... 
A. continue to inform them 
B. give them your contact information 
C. take their opinion into account 
 
2) I'd like to buy my husband a tablet, so I'm keeping my eyes peeled for a 
sale on electronics. 
Keep your eyes peeled means... 
A. actively searching in various places 
B. hoping for something good 
C. watching until something appears 
 
3) When something incredibly unfair happens to me, I find it very hard to 
keep my cool. 
Keep your cool means... 
A. avoid speaking 
B. ignore something 
C. stay calm 
 
4) Celebrities often try to keep a low profile while on vacation so that they 
don't get bothered by photographers and fans. 


Keep a low profile means... 
A. avoid attracting attention 
B. go to remote places 
C. take security measures 
 
5) When I saw that my boss had toilet paper stuck to his shoe, I could barely 
keep a straight face. 
Keep a straight face means... 
A. avoid smiling or laughing 
B. look away from something 
C. take someone seriously 
 
6) I'm sending in my application for a major scholarship - keep your fingers 
crossed for me! 
Keep your fingers crossed means... 
A. help write something 
B. shake hands 
C. wish for good luck 
 
7) She prefers running and swimming over team sports because she likes to 
keep to herself. 
Keep to yourself means... 
A. keep a secret 
B. take care of your health 
C. tend to be solitary 
 
8) If he didn't take medication to keep his disease in check, it would just get 
progressively worse. 


Keep something in check means... 
A. control and restrain it 
B. monitor it 
C. resolve a problem 
 
9) There are so many irregular verbs in English that it's impossible to keep 
them straight! 
Keep things straight means... 
A. create a system for organizing them 
B. understand them clearly without confusing them 
C. use them correctly all the time 
 
10) The guy is on the suspected terrorist list, so the police have been keeping 
tabs on him for years. 
Keep tabs on means... 
A. ask questions 
B. try to capture 
C. watch and monitor 
 
Explanation 
To keep someone posted (A) means to continue to inform them, to update 
them with the most current information about a situation that may change or 
develop over time. Another idiom for this is "keep someone in the loop." 
If you're keeping your eyes peeled, (C) it means you're watching the general 
area until something appears (something you are waiting for or want to 
notice). Another expression for this is to "keep an eye out for something." 
Keep your cool (C) is an informal way to talk about staying calm. The 
opposite is “lose your cool” - that's when you get angry and lose control of 


your attitude/behavior. For staying calm, you can also say, "keep a cool 
head" or "keep a level head." 
To keep a low profile (A) means to do things to avoid attracting attention. 
You keep a low profile when you don't want people to notice you, as in the 
example of celebrities keeping a low profile while on vacation so that they 
won’t constantly be approached and bothered. 
If you keep a straight face, (A) it means you avoid smiling or laughing. We 
usually try to keep a straight face in situations where it would be 
inappropriate to show amusement, or where it would embarrass the other 
person if we started laughing at them. 
To keep your fingers crossed (C) means to wish for good luck. Sometimes 
people will do the literal gesture of crossing two fingers when saying or 
hearing this phrase. You can keep your own fingers crossed (wishing good 
luck for yourself) or you can keep your fingers crossed for someone else 
(wishing good luck for that person). 
A person who keeps to himself/herself (C) tends to be solitary, they prefer 
to spend most of their time alone. Don't get this expression mixed up with the 
phrase "keep it/this/that to yourself," which means to keep a secret. 
To keep something in check (A) means to control or restrain it. Without this 
controlling/restraining action, the thing would progress too much, as in the 
example of a disease being kept in check by medication. 
Keep things straight (B) means to understand them clearly without 
confusing them. When there are many things, or similar things, it can be 
difficult to keep them straight in your head (in your mind/understanding). 
To keep tabs on someone or something (C) is an informal way to describe 
watching and monitoring it over time. We might keep tabs on 
someone/something potentially dangerous (as in the example of a possible 
terrorist) or on something neutral that we just want to know the status of, like 
keeping tabs on your friends through Facebook. 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
keep a low profile 
keep me posted 
keep them straight 
keep a straight face 
keep my fingers crossed 
keep to yourself 
keep it in check 
keep tabs on 
keep your cool 
keep your eyes peeled 
 
1. Crime is on the rise in that neighborhood, so the city is increasing police 
presence there to _______________________. 
2. If something funny happens during a funeral, you should still try to 
_______________________. 
3. It's tempting to _______________________ when you're going through a hard 
time, but support from friends can really help. 
4. Glad to hear your interview went well. I’ll _______________________ that 
you’ll get the job. 
5. OK, her house will be on this street, on the right. _______________________ for 
number 742. 
6. Sally and Sandy are identical twins and I can never _______________________. 
7. The doctor put sensors on my chest to _______________________ my 
heartbeat. 
8. While I was on vacation, my manager would e-mail me occasionally to 
_______________________ on what was happening at work. 
9. Yelling at people won't resolve the problem. You need to learn to 
_______________________. 
10. 
The vice president hasn't given any interviews in the media, it 
looks like he wants to _______________________. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 


Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Describe a time you were keeping your eyes peeled for something. 
2. Talk about a situation in which it was hard for you to keep your cool. 
3. Who is someone you're keeping your fingers crossed for at the moment? 
4. What are some things that you have difficulty keeping straight? 
5. What's something you like to keep tabs on? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net  
 
Practice Quiz Answers

2. keep a straight face 
3. keep to yourself 
4. keep my fingers crossed 
5. keep your eyes peeled 
6. keep them straight 
7. keep tabs on 
8. keep me posted 
9. keep your cool 
10. 
keep a low profile

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 29: Idioms with CALL 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) When my father had a heart attack at a young age, it was the wake-up call 
he needed to take better care of himself. 
A wake-up call means... 
A. an event that brings awareness 
B. beginning to look for other options 
C. when you're convinced by other people 
 
2) That was a close call - the driver wasn't paying attention and nearly hit the 
guy crossing the street. 
A close call means... 
A. a dangerous situation that almost happened 
B. a situation someone doesn't know about 
C. a thing that is difficult to see 
 
3) Duty calls - I've gotta pick up my kids from school. Talk to you later! 
Duty calls means... 
A. being very busy 
B. having to leave for an obligation 
C. receiving a phone call 
 
4) We played soccer for an hour but when it started raining hard, we had to 
call it quits. 


Call it quits means... 
A. delay until later 
B. go home early 
C. stop doing something 
 
5) When a mistake was found in the procedure, the results of the experiment 
were called into question. 
Call into question means... 
A. cancel or ignore 
B. be completely wrong 
C. the possibility of doubt appears 
 
6) I'm not sure which of the top two skaters had the better performance; it's a 
tough call. 
A tough call means... 
A. beyond someone's understanding 
B. difficult to evaluate/decide 
C. not pleasant to watch 
 
7) We can all make suggestions for the promotional campaign, but the 
marketing director is ultimately calling the shots. 
Call the shots means... 
A. control and make the decisions 
B. doing the work 
C. organizing the tasks 
 
8) I used to work as an executive assistant, so I was at the president's beck 
and call. 


To be at someone's beck and call means... 
A. available and ready to obey them 
B. doing everything in their place 
C. working very closely with them 
 
9) Anyone else want me to get them something from the cafe? Last call - I'm 
about to leave. 
Last call means... 
A. almost ready 
B. final opportunity 
C. tell what you want 
 
10) You bought a Toyota? Good call. They're very reliable cars. 
Good call means... 
A. approve of a decision 
B. in the same situation 
C. think positively 
 
Explanation 
A wake-up call (A) is an event that brings awareness - it makes you pay 
attention to something you were previously ignoring or didn't think much 
about. Sudden shocking events or tragedies can often serve as a wake-up call. 
A close call (A) is a dangerous situation that almost happened, but didn't 
happen. It's a potential disaster that came close and was barely avoided. 
If you say duty calls, (B) it means you need to stop what you're doing and go 
take care of an obligation. The word duty is another word for work or a task 
that you must do, and the duty is "calling" you away from your current 
activity. 


The expression call it quits (C) simply means to stop doing something. A 
somewhat similar phrase is "call it a day," which means to stop working for 
the day (and often resume the work tomorrow). 
When something is called into question, (C) it means that the possibility of 
doubt appears - so the thing must be reevaluated to see whether it is true or 
false, good or bad. 
The expression a tough call (B) refers to a situation where it is difficult to 
evaluate or decide. It's often used when two things are very similar, or when 
the situation is very complex and it's not easy to know what is right, true, or 
best. 
If someone is calling the shots, (A) it means he/she is making the main 
decisions. This person has the authority to decide what must be done. 
To be at someone's beck and call (A) means to be available and ready to 
obey that person. It implies that you must always be ready to do everything 
that person asks or orders. 
Last call (B) is simply an informal way to alert people to their final 
opportunity or last chance to get or do something. 
Saying something was a good call (A) means you approve of the decision; you 
think it was a good idea or good choice – as in the example of buying a reliable 
car. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence: 
at my beck and call 
call the shots 
good call 
call into question 
close call 
last call 
call it quits 
duty calls 
tough call 
wake-up call

there are only a few left. 
2. There was only one ____________________ in the game when the ball just 
barely missed the top of the goal. 
3. All the houses we saw were very nice, so it was a ____________________ to 
figure out which one to buy. 
4. I don't expect you to be ____________________, but it would be nice if you 
helped me occasionally. 
5. If a customer gets hurt, it will ____________________ the safety of our 
product. 
6. My sister always wants to ____________________ on our family vacations, but 
she has to learn that she can't always get her way. 
7. I wish I could stay longer, but ____________________; I'm scheduled to work 
tonight. 
8. This environmental disaster is a ____________________ for the country to 
make stricter laws about pollution. 
9. You've been trying to fix the car for hours, but you haven't made any 
progress. It's time to ____________________. 


10. 
____________________ on breaking up with your ex-boyfriend... I 
always thought he was pretty immature. 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
 
Short-Answer Exercises 
1. Have you or someone you know ever experienced a wake-up call? 
2. What's something you've seen that was a close call> 
3. Describe a time when you called it quits. 
4. Talk about a situation that was a tough call. 
5. What's one thing you saw someone else do, which you think was a good 
call? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net

lessons.fullText:
Lesson 30: Idioms with LIKE 
Introductory Quiz 
Guess the correct meaning of each idiom from the context. It's OK if you get a lot 
of answers wrong – what’s important is to do your best in trying to figure it out! 
1) My best friend lives in New York City, and she felt like a fish out of water 
when I took her on a camping trip. 
Like a fish out of water means... 
A. away from one's normal environment 
B. in a dangerous situation 
C. in the middle of nature 
 
2) Barbara's singing is nothing special, but she can dance like nobody's 
business. 
Like nobody's business means... 
A. not professionally 
B. very much or very well 
C. without anybody watching 
 
3) I've never spoken in front of a big audience, and I'm worried that once I'm 
on stage I'll just stand there like a deer in the headlights. 
Like a deer in the headlights means... 
A. difficult to see 
B. paralyzed with fear 
C. the center of attention 
 
4) My mother loves buying unique things, so when I took her to a big antiques 
shop, she was like a kid in a candy store. 


Like a kid in a candy store means... 
A. excited 
B. hungry 
C. immature 
 
5) Basketball is such a fast-paced game for fans, but baseball is like watching 
paint dry. 
Like watching paint dry means... 
A. boring 
B. easy 
C. simple 
 
6) Trying to find a single document in these disorganized boxes of archives is 
like looking for a needle in a haystack. 
Like looking for a needle in a haystack means... 
A. almost impossible to find 
B. making a big mess 
C. needing a lot of help 
 
7) Alan once got sick from eating pork, and he's avoided it like the plague 
ever since. 
Avoid it like the plague means... 
A. avoid it completely 
B. avoid it for a good reason 
C. avoid it temporarily 
 
8) I can't stand taking the subway at rush hour because everyone's packed 
like sardines - you barely have room to breathe. 


Packed like sardines means... 
A. extremely crowded 
B. in a rush 
C. smell bad 
 
9) When I brought out a big bowl of candy, all the kids came running like 
moths to a flame. 
Like moths to a flame means... 
A. there are too many 
B. with intense interest/desire 
C. without thinking 
 
10) My son is quite adaptable; when we moved to another country with a very 
different culture, he took to it like a duck to water. 
Take to it like a duck to water means... 
A. do many different activities 
B. get used to something easily 
C. travel in the local area 
 
Explanation 
The natural home of a fish is in the water - so to feel/be like a fish out of 
water (A) means to feel out of place, because you are outside your normal 
environment. This feeling can be a little awkward or uncomfortable because 
you are not used to the situation. 
To do something like nobody’s business (B) means to do it a lot (very 
intensely) or do it very well, have a lot of skills in that activity – as in the 
example, where Barbara can’t sing very well, but she is an extremely talented 
dancer. 


This animal is called a deer. If a deer is crossing the street and a car 
approaches with its headlights on, the deer will often "freeze" (stop moving) 
because it is afraid. If you are like a deer in the headlights, (B) it means you 
are paralyzed with fear or surprise. 
 
A kid (child) in a candy store (A) would be excited and eager, wanting to eat 
all the candy - so this expression is used to describe when someone is very 
excited, especially when they have the opportunity to try or buy many 
different things that they love. 
Like watching paint dry (A) is a way to describe something that is extremely 
boring. Paint takes a long time to dry and there would be nothing interesting 
about watching the process. 
 
A needle is very small, and a haystack is a pile of dry grass often found on 
farms. It would be very difficult - almost impossible - to find a single needle 
hidden in a large haystack, so “like looking for a needle in a haystack” (A) is 
used to describe anything that's almost impossible to find. 


The word plague refers to any disease that is dangerous and can spread from 
person to person. If there was a plague in your area, you would do everything 
possible to avoid catching the disease! So the expression avoid something 
like the plague (A) means to avoid it completely, avoid it at all costs. 
Sardines are a small type of fish that is often sold in cans or tins, in which 
there are many sardines in a small space. When we say people are packed 
like sardines, (A) it means the space is extremely crowded and 
uncomfortable. 
 
Flying insects like moths are attracted to light, such as the flame of a fire. 
When people come to something like moths to a flame, (B) it means they 
come close with intense interest or desire. 
  
 


A duck can swim in water easily and naturally. When we say someone "took 
to (a situation/activity) like a duck to water," (B) it means the person 
adapted or got used to the situation/activity easily and naturally, without 
difficulty. 
 
 
Practice Quiz 
Choose the correct idiom to complete each sentence:

plague 
 
like a kid in a candy store 
like nobody's 
business 
like a deer in the 
headlights 
 
like looking for a needle in 
a haystack

dry 
like a fish out of 
water 
like moths to a flame 
packed like sardines 
 
took to it like a duck 
to water 
 
1. A handsome guy with a fancy car attracts women 
_____________________________. 
2. Carlos has been spending money _____________________________ lately, and 
he's almost run out of savings. 


3. I absolutely love libraries. I'm _____________________________ - there are so 
many great books to check out! 
4. We managed to fit six people into a small taxi, but we were 
_____________________________. 
5. I thought it would be hard to learn to ride a motorcycle, but surprisingly 
I _____________________________. 
6. Identifying the criminal in a city of 3 million people is 
_____________________________. 
7. These four-hour meetings at work are the worst part of my week. 
They're _____________________________. 
8. My brothers are so lazy. They hate exercise and 
_____________________________. 
9. When Tina told Ron she was attracted to him, he looked 
_____________________________ and couldn't think of anything to say. 
10. 
I need to learn some better social skills so that I'm not 
_____________________________ at big parties. 
 
Answers are at the end of this lesson. 
 
 
 
 
 
 


Short-Answer Exercises 
1. What's something you avoid like the plague? 
2. Describe a situation in which you feel like a fish out of water. 
3. What's an activity that you think is like watching paint dry? 
4. What's something you can do like nobody's business? 
5. Talk about a time you were like a deer in the headlights. 
6. Have you ever seen someone take to a situation/activity like a duck to 
water? 
If you want correction / feedback, you can e-mail me your writing at 
homework@espressoenglish.net
